title: Capstone: A Close Reading Argued from the Text
bigQuestion: How do you build an honest argument about what a biblical passage does and means, using the text, its world and its readers, without telling anyone what to believe?

story.title: One Passage, Two Translations, Three Commentaries
story.kicker: A senior picks the book of Ruth, opens two Bibles and three commentaries, and finds that the hardest part is deciding what she thinks.
paragraphs: Maya needed a passage for her capstone. She had liked Ruth when the class read it in the fall: four chapters, a famine, two widows walking back to Bethlehem, a field, a night on a threshing floor, a wedding and a baby. She chose Ruth 1:16–17, the speech in which Ruth refuses to leave her mother-in-law Naomi. She wrote her question on an index card: what is Ruth promising, and to whom? Her teacher said that a good question is one the text can answer and thoughtful readers have answered differently. That one seemed to fit.

She read the speech in the King James Version first, because its cadence was the one she half knew: whither thou goest, I will go. Then she read it in the Jewish Publication Society translation of 1917, which was close, and in a modern translation from the library, which was plainer. One line stopped her. The KJV has Ruth say 'thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.' A footnote in the modern version said the Hebrew sentence has no verb; it reads more like 'your people, my people; your God, my God.' Maya wrote in her notes: is this a vow, or a statement of fact? That was already an argument.

The commentaries pulled in three directions. Rashi, the eleventh-century French rabbi, read the whole speech as a conversation about conversion: Naomi warns Ruth about the commandments, and Ruth accepts each one. A Christian commentary pointed to Matthew 1:5, where Ruth appears in the genealogy of Jesus, and read her as a Gentile brought into God's people. A university commentary set the book in the Persian period and read it as a quiet answer to Ezra 9–10, where foreign wives are sent away. Each reading used the same seventeen words.

Maya's first draft tried to say all three were right. Her teacher handed it back with one note: what do you think the text is doing? She went back to the Hebrew word hesed, which appears in Ruth 1:8, 2:20 and 3:10 and which the KJV renders as kindness. Her thesis became this: Ruth's speech is the book's first act of hesed, a loyalty that goes past what any law requires, and the book keeps measuring every other character against it. She could support that from the text. She could say how Rashi, the Christian commentary and the Persian-period reading each fit or strained against it. And she did not need to decide whether God had anything to do with it.

Her presentation was seven minutes long. A classmate who was Jewish said Rashi's reading had felt right to him and asked why she had not gone further with it. Another, who was not religious, asked whether hesed was really different from ordinary kindness. Maya answered both from the text, page open. That, her teacher said afterward, is the whole course in one afternoon: a passage, its words, its readers and a student who can argue about it fairly.
story.think: Maya's first draft said all three commentaries were right, and her teacher sent it back. What is the difference between being fair to other readings and having no argument of your own?

lessons.title: A Passage and a Question
lessons.mainIdea: A capstone begins with a passage short enough to read closely and a question that the text can answer and that its readers have answered differently.
reading: The first decision is size. A capstone passage should be something you can read in full several times and hold in your head: a *pericope*, the scholars' word for a self-contained unit, such as a psalm, a parable, a speech, a law or a scene. Ruth 1:16–17 is two verses. The parable of the prodigal son is twenty-two. Genesis 22, the binding of Isaac, is nineteen. Psalm 137 is nine. A whole chapter of Romans is too much for one argument; a single verse is often too little to show how it works. Choose the unit the text itself marks off by a change of speaker, place or subject.

The second decision is the question. A weak question can be answered by looking something up: who was Ruth's husband? A weak question of another kind cannot be answered from the text at all: did this really happen, or is this the word of God? Those questions belong to history and to faith, and this course leaves them there. A strong question asks what the text is doing and how: what is Ruth promising, and to whom? Why does Psalm 137 end the way it does? What does the older brother's silence do in Luke 15? Strong questions have a range of defensible answers, and readers over the centuries have in fact given different ones.

Test your question against three checks before you commit. Can the text answer it, at least in part, from its own words? Have Jewish, Christian or academic readers actually disagreed about it, so that you will have something to weigh? Can you state, in one sentence, what would count as evidence? If a question fails a check, narrow it or move it. Write the passage, the translation you started with, and the question on one card and keep it in front of you. Every later step in the capstone returns to that card.

words.d: a self-contained unit of a text, such as a psalm, parable or scene, marked off by a change of speaker, place or subject
a final project that draws together the skills of a whole course
able to be supported with evidence from the text and its world

look.title: Sort the Questions
look.text: Five questions about Genesis 22, the binding of Isaac: (1) How old was Isaac? (2) Did this event happen? (3) Why does the narrator repeat the phrase 'and the two of them went together' in verses 6 and 8? (4) Is God good? (5) How have Jewish and Christian readers explained Abraham's silence?
look.prompt: Which questions can the text answer? Which belong to history or faith and stay outside this course? Which would make the strongest capstone question, and why?

check.q: What is a pericope?
choices: A footnote in a study Bible
A self-contained unit of text such as a parable or psalm
A commentary by a rabbi
A translation made from the Greek
check.why: Scholars use pericope for a passage the text itself marks off, the right size for close reading.

check.q: Which is the strongest capstone question?
choices: Who was Ruth's first husband?
Is the book of Ruth true?
What is Ruth promising in 1:16–17, and to whom?
How many verses are in Ruth?
check.why: It asks what the text is doing, can be answered from its words, and readers have answered it differently; the others are lookups or belong to faith.

check.q: Why does the course leave the question 'Did this really happen?' outside the capstone?
choices: Because scholars have settled it
Because it belongs to history and faith rather than to the text's own words
Because the Bible does not describe events
Because students are not allowed to ask it
check.why: The capstone argues from the text; questions of historical fact and religious truth are attributed to their fields, not decided in a public school essay.

lessons.title: Two Translations Side by Side
lessons.mainIdea: Reading a passage in two translations exposes the choices every translator makes and points you toward the words that carry the argument.
reading: No translation is neutral. Every one chooses between words, and the choices add up to a reading. Set two translations of your passage in parallel columns and mark every difference, however small. Some will be style: thee and thou against you. Some will be vocabulary: kindness against loyalty, virgin against young woman, charity against love. Some will be punctuation and line breaks, which the Hebrew and Greek manuscripts largely lack. Each difference is a place where the translator had to decide, and each is a possible doorway into your argument.

Translations sit on a spectrum. At one end is *formal equivalence*, which follows the words and order of the original as closely as English allows; the King James Version (1611), the American Standard Version (1901) and the JPS Tanakh of 1917 lean this way. At the other end is *dynamic equivalence*, which aims at the meaning of a sentence in natural English; many twentieth-century versions lean this way. Neither is more faithful in every case. A formal translation keeps a strange phrase strange; a dynamic one may explain it and hide the strangeness. For a capstone, one of each is the most useful pair.

Public-domain translations can be quoted freely. Modern ones such as the NIV, NRSV, ESV or NJPS (1985) are under copyright, so describe or paraphrase them with a citation. When you find a difference that matters, do not stop at the English. A study Bible's notes, an interlinear text or a good lexicon will tell you the underlying Hebrew or Greek word and its range of meaning. Then you can say, with evidence, that the King James has one reading and the JPS another. You can also say whether the word behind both can bear either.

words.d: a translation approach that follows the words and order of the original closely, as the King James Version does
a translation approach that aims at the meaning of each sentence in natural English
a dictionary of an ancient language, such as Hebrew or Greek, giving each word's range of meanings
free of copyright, so that a text may be quoted and reprinted by anyone

look.title: One Verse, Two Columns
look.text: Isaiah 7:14, King James Version (1611): Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. Jewish Publication Society (1917): Therefore the Lord Himself shall give you a sign: behold, the young woman shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. The Hebrew word is almah.
look.prompt: Mark every difference. Which one carries a difference in reading? What would you need to look up before you could argue about it, and whose readings would you have to attribute?

check.q: What does formal equivalence mean?
choices: A translation that follows the words and order of the original closely
A translation made by a committee
A translation into formal, polite English
A translation that explains each sentence in natural English
check.why: Formal equivalence stays close to the original's wording, as the KJV and JPS 1917 do; dynamic equivalence aims at natural meaning.

check.q: Why should a capstone paraphrase rather than quote the NRSV or NJPS 1985?
choices: Because they are inaccurate
Because they are written in Hebrew
Because they are under copyright, unlike the KJV or JPS 1917
Because schools are not allowed to own them
check.why: Modern translations are copyrighted; public-domain versions such as the KJV, ASV, WEB and JPS 1917 may be quoted freely.

check.q: What is the best next step when two translations differ on a key word?
choices: Choose the older translation
Choose the newer translation
Drop the word from the argument
Look up the underlying Hebrew or Greek word and its range of meaning
check.why: The difference points to the original word; a lexicon or study note shows what it can mean, which is evidence.

lessons.title: Genre and Shape
lessons.mainIdea: Naming a passage's genre and mapping its structure tells you what kind of claims it can make and where its weight falls.
reading: Every passage belongs to a *genre*, a kind of writing with its own rules. A law states a case and a consequence. A psalm addresses God in parallel lines. A parable tells a short story that turns on a surprise. A prophetic oracle speaks in God's name to a specific audience. A letter answers a situation the reader can only partly see. A genealogy makes claims by inclusion and order. Readers who mistake the genre misread the text: a parable is not a report, and a lament is not a doctrine. Name the genre first and say how you know.

Then map the *structure*. Where does the passage begin and end, and what marks the borders? Who speaks, and to whom, and when does the speaker change? What is repeated? Hebrew narrative and poetry love repetition, and a repeated word, called a *Leitwort* by scholars, often carries the theme: 'went' and 'return' in Ruth 1, 'see' in Genesis 22, 'remember' in Psalm 137. Many passages fold in the middle, a pattern called *chiasm*, with the key line at the center. Draw the shape on paper: an outline, a table of speakers, or a diagram of matching parts.

Shape is evidence. Ruth's speech falls into pairs: where you go I go, where you lodge I lodge, your people my people, your God my God. Then it breaks the pattern with death and burial. That break is where the reader is meant to feel the weight. The parable of the prodigal son gives the older brother the last speech and the father the last word. It never tells us whether the brother goes in. That silence is a choice by the author. Your capstone should name at least one feature of shape and say what it does.

words.d: a kind of writing with its own rules, such as law, psalm, parable, oracle, letter or genealogy
the shape of a passage: its borders, speakers, repetitions and turning points
a leading word repeated through a passage to carry its theme; a term from the scholars Buber and Rosenzweig
a pattern in which the second half of a passage mirrors the first, with the key idea at the center

look.title: The Shape of Ruth's Speech
look.text: And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God: Where thou diest, will I die, and there will I be buried: the LORD do so to me, and more also, if ought but death part thee and me.
look.prompt: Count the paired clauses. Where does the pattern break? What does Ruth add at the end that turns a statement into an oath, and how does that change what she is promising?

check.q: Why does genre matter for reading a passage?
choices: Because each genre is in a different language
Because genre determines what kind of claims a passage can make
Because only narrative counts as literature
Because genre tells you the date of a book
check.why: A parable is not a report and a lament is not a doctrine; mistaking the genre misreads the text.

check.q: What is a Leitwort?
choices: A word repeated through a passage that carries its theme
The first word of a biblical book
A German translation of the Bible
A word with no known meaning
check.why: Buber and Rosenzweig used the term for leading words such as 'return' in Ruth 1.

check.q: What is a chiasm?
choices: A genealogy in reverse order
A psalm sung by two choirs
A pattern in which the second half mirrors the first around a center
A break between two speakers
check.why: In a chiasm the parts fold around a central line, which often holds the key idea.

lessons.title: The World Behind the Text
lessons.mainIdea: Historical context, stated carefully and with 'c.' where dates are uncertain, explains what a passage's first hearers would have taken for granted.
reading: A passage carries assumptions its first audience shared and you do not. Ruth's readers knew what gleaning was, that a widow without sons was in danger, and that Moab was Israel's neighbor and sometime enemy across the Jordan (Deuteronomy 23:3 bars Moabites from the assembly). Psalm 137's readers knew Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BCE. Luke's readers knew that pigs were unclean to Jews and that a Roman father's authority was nearly absolute. Reconstructing that world is the work of *historical context*, and it is where a capstone most often goes wrong by overstating.

Use dates with care. Scholars date the book of Ruth anywhere from the early monarchy to the Persian period, roughly the tenth to the fourth century BCE. The honest sentence is this: most scholars date Ruth to the Persian period, though some argue for an earlier date. Write 'c.' before any date that is not fixed. Attribute claims about history to the kind of evidence behind them: archaeology, other ancient texts, the language of the passage. Never say 'the Bible proves' or 'archaeology disproves.' Say what the text says and what the evidence suggests, and keep the two apart.

Reliable context comes from named sources: a university-press introduction, a study Bible's notes, an encyclopedia entry with an author. Avoid unsigned websites and any source that tells you what the text must mean before it tells you what the text says. Limit yourself to the context that bears on your question. If your question is about Ruth's promise, the price of barley in Bethlehem does not help; the law of the *levirate* marriage in Deuteronomy 25 and the status of a foreign widow do. Two or three well-chosen facts, cited, beat a page of background.

words.d: the time, place, customs and events that a passage's first audience would have known
the era c. 539–332 BCE when Judah was a province of the Persian Empire, to which many scholars date Ruth
the custom in Deuteronomy 25 by which a man marries his dead brother's widow to carry on the family line
gathering grain left behind by harvesters, a right of the poor under Leviticus 19:9–10

look.title: Dates a Reader of Ruth Needs
look.cite: Standard chronologies in university-press introductions to the Hebrew Bible; several dates are approximate
look.prompt: If Ruth was written in the Persian period, which of these events were recent memory for its first readers? How might that change what a story about a Moabite wife was doing?

check.q: What is the honest way to state the date of the book of Ruth?
choices: It was written by Samuel in the eleventh century BCE
It was certainly written in 450 BCE
Its date is unknown, so it should not be discussed
Most scholars date it to the Persian period, though some argue for an earlier date
check.why: Scholars disagree; the capstone reports the range and the majority view with attribution rather than a single certain date.

check.q: What is levirate marriage?
choices: Marriage between Israelites and Moabites
A man marrying his dead brother's widow to continue the family line
A wedding held at the threshing floor
A marriage arranged by a priest
check.why: Deuteronomy 25 describes the levirate custom, which lies behind the redemption scene in Ruth 4.

check.q: Which source of context is most reliable for a capstone?
choices: An unsigned website that explains the passage's true meaning
A university-press introduction or a signed encyclopedia entry
A friend's memory of a sermon
A film version of the story
check.why: Named academic sources can be cited and checked; unsigned sites that decide meaning in advance cannot.

lessons.title: Key Words in Hebrew and Greek
lessons.mainIdea: Tracing one key word through your passage and the rest of the Bible often supplies the strongest evidence in a capstone.
reading: Behind every English Bible stand Hebrew and Aramaic for the Hebrew Bible and Greek for the New Testament. You do not need to read those languages to use them. A *concordance* lists every place a word appears; a lexicon gives its range; a study Bible's notes flag words the translators argued over. Start with the two or three words in your passage that carry the most weight, and find the original word behind each. Then see where else it appears and how it is translated there.

The Hebrew word *hesed* is the classic example. The King James renders it kindness in Ruth 1:8, 2:20 and 3:10, mercy in Psalm 23:6 and lovingkindness in Psalm 36:7. Scholars describe it as loyal love, the faithfulness owed within a relationship, whether between people or between God and Israel, and note that it usually goes beyond what is required. If your thesis is that Ruth's speech is an act of hesed, the word's other uses are your evidence, and you can show that the book applies the word to Ruth, to Boaz and to God.

Greek offers similar cases. *Logos* in John 1:1 means word, reason or speech, and translators have chosen among them. *Agape* in 1 Corinthians 13 was charity in the King James and love in nearly every later version, a change that altered how English speakers hear the chapter. *Metanoia*, translated repentance, means literally a change of mind. When you cite a word study, name the tool you used and the verses you checked, and do not claim more than the evidence shows. A word's root does not fix its meaning; its use in context does.

words.d: an index listing every place a word appears in the Bible
a Hebrew word for loyal love or faithful kindness, translated kindness, mercy or lovingkindness in the King James Version
a Greek word meaning word, reason or speech, used of Jesus in John 1:1
a Greek word for love, rendered charity in the King James Version of 1 Corinthians 13

look.title: The Same Word, Two Verses Apart
look.text: And Naomi said unto her two daughters in law, Go, return each to her mother's house: the LORD deal kindly with you, as ye have dealt with the dead, and with me. (1:8) … Blessed be he of the LORD, who hath not left off his kindness to the living and to the dead. (2:20)
look.cite: Ruth 1:8 and 2:20, King James Version (1611); the Hebrew word in both is hesed
look.prompt: In 1:8 Naomi asks God to show hesed as Ruth has shown it; in 2:20 she blesses either Boaz or God for hesed. What does the book seem to be saying by using one word for people and for God?

check.q: What is a concordance?
choices: A translation that agrees with another
An index of every place a word appears in the Bible
A commentary written by a rabbi
A list of the books in the canon
check.why: A concordance lets you trace a word such as hesed through the whole text.

check.q: How does the King James Version translate hesed in Ruth?
choices: Kindness
Covenant
Righteousness
Peace
check.why: The KJV uses kindness in Ruth 1:8, 2:20 and 3:10; the same word is mercy in Psalm 23:6.

check.q: Which change in translating 1 Corinthians 13 altered how English readers hear the chapter?
choices: Faith became trust
Prophecy became preaching
Charity became love
Glass became mirror
check.why: The KJV's charity for agape became love in nearly all later versions.

lessons.title: Jewish, Christian and Academic Readers
lessons.mainIdea: Every capstone consults at least three kinds of readers, Jewish, Christian and academic, and reports each reading in its own terms with attribution.
reading: The Bible has been read closely for more than two thousand years, and a capstone joins that conversation rather than starting it. Jewish reading reaches back to the rabbis of the *Midrash* and Talmud, through medieval commentators such as Rashi (1040–1105) and Ibn Ezra, to modern scholars. Rashi's commentary, printed beside the text in traditional Jewish Bibles, explains word by word and draws on earlier midrash. On Ruth 1:16 he reads Ruth's replies as answers to Naomi's instruction in the laws a convert must accept. That is a Jewish reading, and it should be reported as one.

Christian reading runs from the New Testament's own use of the Hebrew Bible, through the church fathers such as Augustine, the medieval fourfold sense, the Reformers Luther and Calvin, to modern commentaries of every denomination. Christian readers of Ruth often note Matthew 1:5, where Ruth stands in the genealogy of Jesus, and read her as a Gentile brought into the people of God. That is a Christian reading, and a Jewish reader would not share the frame. Neither is the text's own statement. Your job is to describe each as its readers would recognize it.

Academic reading, from the nineteenth century on, asks when and why a text was written. It asks how the text fits its world and how it works as literature. It does not assume the text's religious claims are true or false. Scholars of every faith and none work this way, and they disagree among themselves. A Persian-period reading of Ruth as a reply to Ezra's ban on foreign wives is one proposal; others date the book earlier and read it differently. Cite at least one reader of each kind by name, title and year. Then say where they agree, where they part, and which of their observations your own argument can use.

words.d: rabbinic interpretation of the Bible, often filling gaps in the story, collected from about the third century CE on
Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040–1105), a French rabbi whose commentary on the Bible and Talmud is still printed beside the text
early Christian writers of roughly the second to eighth centuries, such as Augustine, whose readings shaped later Christian interpretation
academic study of the Bible's history, language and literature that does not assume its religious claims are true or false

look.title: Readers of Ruth Across Time
rows: Ruth translated into Greek (Septuagint), c. BCE
Ruth Rabbah (midrash on Ruth) compiled, c. CE
Robert Alter, The Hebrew Bible: A Translation with Commentary, CE
look.cite: Standard dating; Ruth Rabbah's compilation date is uncertain and given roughly
look.prompt: Which of these readers would a capstone cite as Jewish, which as Christian and which as academic? Which categories overlap?

check.q: Who was Rashi?
choices: A church father who wrote in Latin
A Persian-period scribe
A nineteenth-century German scholar
A French rabbi (1040–1105) whose commentary is printed beside the biblical text
check.why: Rashi's word-by-word commentary is a standard Jewish reading; Augustine was a church father and Wellhausen a German scholar.

check.q: Which verse do Christian readers often cite when reading Ruth?
choices: Deuteronomy 23:3
Matthew 1:5, where Ruth appears in the genealogy of Jesus
Ezra 9:1
Psalm 137:1
check.why: Matthew's genealogy includes Ruth, and Christian readers build on that; the frame is not shared by Jewish readers.

check.q: What marks an academic reading of a passage?
choices: It proves the text is true
It proves the text is false
It studies the text's history, language and literature without assuming its religious claims are true or false
It is written only by people of no religion
check.why: Critical scholarship is practiced by people of every faith and none and sets the question of religious truth aside.

lessons.title: A Thesis About What the Text Does
lessons.mainIdea: A capstone thesis makes a claim about what the passage does and means that is specific, arguable and answerable from the text, not a claim about whether it is true.
reading: A *thesis* is one sentence that answers your question and that someone could reasonably dispute. Compare three sentences about Ruth 1:16–17. 'Ruth's speech is beautiful' is a reaction, not a claim. 'Ruth's speech shows that God rewards loyalty' is a claim about God, which the capstone cannot argue from a public-school desk. 'Ruth's speech is the book's first act of hesed, and the book measures every other character against it' is a claim about the text: specific, arguable and testable against the words on the page. That is the kind of sentence you want.

Good theses tend to use verbs about what a text does: shows, withholds, repeats, reverses, invites, refuses. They name a feature you found in the reading stage. That might be a repeated word, a break in pattern, a silence or a translation choice. Then they say what it accomplishes. A thesis can be about meaning as readers have found it, so long as the reading is attributed. For example: read alongside Ezra 9–10, as many scholars do, Ruth's speech becomes a quiet argument that a foreign woman can be a model Israelite. The attribution is part of the thesis.

Draft the thesis early and expect to revise it. Maya's first thesis was that all three commentaries were right, which is not a claim. Her second was that Ruth converts to Judaism, which is Rashi's reading, not hers, and which uses a later category. Her third, about hesed, came from the text and let her use all three readers as witnesses. Write your thesis on the index card under your question. If the evidence you gather does not fit it, change the thesis, not the evidence.

words.d: the one-sentence claim an essay argues for; in a capstone, a claim about what the text does and means
open to reasonable disagreement, so that evidence is needed to support it
a statement put forward as true and to be supported by evidence

look.title: Four Sentences About Psalm 137
look.text: (1) Psalm 137 is disturbing. (2) Psalm 137 proves that God wanted Babylon destroyed. (3) Psalm 137 moves from memory to oath to curse, and its final verse is the pain of verse 1 turned outward. (4) Psalm 137 was written in Babylon in 586 BCE by a Levite singer.
look.prompt: Which sentence is a reaction, which is a claim about God, which is a historical claim stated too confidently, and which is a workable thesis? Rewrite one of the weak ones into a workable thesis.

check.q: Which sentence is a workable capstone thesis?
choices: The parable of the prodigal son is my favorite passage
The parable of the prodigal son proves that God forgives
The parable of the prodigal son gives the father the last word and leaves the older brother's choice open, so that the hearer must finish the story
The parable of the prodigal son was told in 30 CE
check.why: It claims something specific about what the text does that can be tested against Luke 15; the others are a reaction, a claim about God and an overconfident date.

check.q: What made Maya's second thesis, that Ruth converts to Judaism, a problem?
choices: It was Rashi's reading stated as her own and used a later category
It was too short
It was not about Ruth
It quoted the wrong translation
check.why: A thesis must be the student's own claim about the text; a reader's interpretation should be attributed, not adopted as fact.

check.q: What should you do when your evidence does not fit your thesis?
choices: Leave the evidence out
Add more adjectives to the thesis
Choose a different passage
Change the thesis to fit the evidence
check.why: The text is the authority in a close reading; the thesis serves the evidence, not the reverse.

lessons.title: Evidence and Citation
lessons.mainIdea: Evidence in a capstone means quoted or paraphrased text, features of its shape and language, and attributed readings, each cited by book, chapter and verse or by author, title and year.
reading: Evidence from the text comes first. Quote the words you are arguing from, in a named translation, and cite them by book, chapter and verse, with the translation in parentheses on first use: Ruth 1:16 (KJV). A colon separates chapter and verse, a dash joins a range, and a semicolon separates references: Ruth 1:8; 2:20; 3:10. Use standard book abbreviations if your teacher asks; the Society of Biblical Literature's handbook is the usual guide. When you paraphrase a copyrighted translation, say so: 'the NJPS (1985) renders the word as loyalty.' Quote only as much as you need and then explain what it shows.

Evidence from the text's world and its readers is cited like any other source. A commentary is cited by author, title and year, and by page or verse: Robert Alter, The Hebrew Bible (2019), on Ruth 1:16. Rashi is cited as Rashi on Ruth 1:16, with the edition you used. A study Bible's note is cited by the Bible's name and year and the note's verse. Your teacher will name the citation style, usually MLA or Chicago; whichever it is, the reader must be able to find every source you used. A claim without a source is an opinion, and a source without a page is a rumor.

Weigh the evidence as you present it. Strongest is the passage's own wording, structure and repeated words, which any reader can check. Next is the wider text, such as other uses of hesed or the law in Deuteronomy 25. Then comes context from the ancient world, always with 'c.' and attribution. Last are the readers, who are witnesses to how the text has been understood rather than proof of what it means. A paragraph that quotes a verse, names a feature, cites a reader and then states what all of that shows is the basic unit of a capstone essay.

words.d: the reference that lets a reader find your source: book, chapter and verse, or author, title and year
restating a passage in your own words, with a citation, rather than quoting it
the main scholarly association for biblical studies, whose handbook sets standard abbreviations and citation forms
the text itself, as opposed to a secondary source that comments on it

look.title: Fix the Citations
look.text: A draft paragraph: 'In Ruth, Ruth says she will go wherever Naomi goes. The Bible says this is loyalty. Rashi says it is about conversion. A scholar says the book is from the Persian period. So the speech is about hesed.'
look.prompt: Rewrite the paragraph with a quoted verse and translation, a chapter-and-verse citation, a named reader with title and year, and an attributed historical claim with 'c.' Which sentence in the original was not evidence at all?

check.q: Which citation is complete for a quoted verse on first use?
choices: Ruth, chapter one
Ruth 1:16 (KJV)
The Bible, page 240
Ruth 1, the loyalty verse
check.why: Book, chapter, verse and translation let any reader find the exact words.

check.q: Which kind of evidence is strongest in a close reading?
choices: A commentary's opinion
A date from the ancient world
The passage's own wording and structure
A film adaptation
check.why: The words and shape of the passage can be checked by any reader; commentaries are witnesses to readings, not proof of meaning.

check.q: How should a capstone handle a modern copyrighted translation such as the NJPS (1985)?
choices: Quote it freely without citation
Ignore it
Copy its footnotes as your own
Paraphrase or describe its rendering with a citation
check.why: Copyrighted translations are described or paraphrased and cited; public-domain versions may be quoted.

lessons.title: Other Readings, Fairly Stated
lessons.mainIdea: A strong capstone states the best case for readings it does not adopt, in their readers' own terms, and explains why its thesis still stands.
reading: An argument that ignores other readings is a sermon. The capstone asks you to present at least two readings that differ from your own, and to present each so well that a person who holds it would say, yes, that is what I think. This is sometimes called *steelmanning*, the opposite of attacking a weak version of a view. For Ruth, Maya had to state Rashi's conversion reading with its evidence, the Christian genealogy reading with Matthew 1:5, and the Persian-period reading with Ezra 9–10, before she said how her hesed thesis related to each.

There are three honest ways to respond to a reading you do not adopt. You can show that it depends on a frame the text does not supply, such as a later legal category or a later book, while granting that it is coherent within that frame. You can show that it accounts for part of the passage but not for the feature your thesis explains, such as the break in Ruth's pairs. Or you can absorb it: Maya found that all three readers had noticed Ruth's loyalty and could be cited as support. What you may not do is call a reading stupid, or say a tradition is wrong about God.

The language of fairness is attribution and comparison. 'Jewish tradition reads', 'Christian interpreters have often held', 'many scholars argue', 'on this reading'. Compare readings to each other and to the text, never to the truth. If a reader relies on a translation choice, say so; if a reader has textual evidence you lack, say that too. A capstone earns trust by the way it treats the views it sets aside. The reader who disagrees with your thesis should still finish your essay feeling accurately described.

words.d: stating a view you do not hold in its strongest form before responding to it
an interpretation of a passage that differs from the one an essay argues for
the set of assumptions, such as a tradition's laws or later books, through which a reader interprets a passage

look.title: Three Readings of One Silence
look.text: Luke 15 ends with the father telling the older son that his brother was dead and is alive again. It does not say whether the older son goes in. Reading A: the parable is aimed at the Pharisees of Luke 15:2, and the open ending is an invitation to them. Reading B: the open ending shows the father's love does not depend on the brother's answer. Reading C: Luke shaped the ending to make his Gentile readers see themselves as the welcomed son.
look.prompt: State each reading in its strongest form and name what it explains. Then pick one as your thesis and respond to the other two fairly.

check.q: What does steelmanning mean?
choices: Stating a view you disagree with in its strongest form before responding
Refusing to consider other readings
Building an argument out of many short quotations
Choosing the oldest available reading
check.why: Steelmanning is the fair presentation of counter-readings, the opposite of attacking a weak version.

check.q: Which response to a counter-reading is not acceptable in a capstone?
choices: Showing it depends on a frame the text does not supply
Showing it explains part of the passage but not the key feature
Declaring that the tradition behind it is wrong about God
Absorbing its observations as support
check.why: The capstone compares readings to the text and to each other, never to religious truth.

check.q: What phrase shows proper attribution?
choices: Everyone knows that
The truth is that
It is obvious that
Many scholars argue that
check.why: Attribution names whose reading is being reported; the other phrases assert without a source.

lessons.title: Essay, Presentation and Rubric
lessons.mainIdea: The capstone is delivered twice, as a written essay and as a short presentation with the text open, and both are scored on the same rubric.
reading: The essay runs about four to six pages. It opens with the passage quoted in full in a named translation and the question. It states the thesis by the end of the first page. Its body paragraphs follow the order of the method: genre and shape, key words, context, readers, then the argument that ties them to the thesis, then the counter-readings and your response. It closes by saying what the reading shows and what it leaves open. Every paragraph has at least one citation. The bibliography lists the translations used, at least one Jewish, one Christian and one academic reader, and any context source.

The presentation is five to seven minutes, with the passage on the screen or on paper in front of everyone. Read the passage aloud in one translation. State the question and thesis. Show one piece of evidence from the text closely, such as the break in Ruth's pairs, one word study and one reader. Then take questions with the text open, and answer from it. The presentation is not the essay read aloud; it is the argument made in a room, where a classmate can ask why you chose one reading over another and you can point to the verse.

The rubric scores five things equally: the question and thesis; evidence from the text; use of context and readers; fairness to other readings; and clarity, including citations and plain sentences. A capstone that argues something small and supports it fully outscores one that claims much and supports little. Fairness is scored as strictly as evidence. An essay that misrepresents a tradition, states a belief as fact or ranks one tradition's reading above another loses points there even if its reading of the text is strong.

words.d: a scoring guide that names what is being judged and describes each level of quality
the list of sources an essay used, in a standard citation style
a paragraph in the middle of an essay that presents one piece of evidence and explains what it shows

look.title: The Capstone Rubric
look.cite: Course rubric for The Bible, K–12, Architecture of Grace (2026)
look.prompt: Fairness carries as many points as evidence. Why might a course taught in a public school weight it that way? Which criterion would Maya's first draft have scored lowest on?

check.q: What must a capstone essay contain in its first page?
choices: A summary of every commentary
The passage quoted in a named translation, the question and the thesis
A biography of the author
A defense of the Bible's accuracy
check.why: The opening sets the text, the question and the claim; the rest of the essay supports them.

check.q: How is the presentation different from the essay?
choices: It uses a different passage
It does not need citations
It is the argument made aloud with the text open, ending in questions answered from the text
It is longer than the essay
check.why: The presentation tests whether the student can argue in a room with the passage in front of everyone.

check.q: What does the rubric do when an essay states a belief as fact?
choices: Adds points for confidence
Ignores it if the reading is strong
Removes the essay from the course
Deducts points under fairness even if the textual reading is strong
check.why: Fairness is scored as strictly as evidence; attribution is part of the assignment.

lessons.title: Reading a Sacred Text in a Public School
lessons.mainIdea: Studying the Bible in a public school means reading a text that is sacred to many classmates as literature and history, respecting their beliefs without adopting or dismissing them.
reading: This course has read a book that is scripture to Jews and Christians. Muslims honor it as earlier revelation. People of every tradition and of none read it as literature and history. The 1963 Schempp decision made that study legal in a public school, when it is presented objectively as part of a secular program. Objectivity does not mean pretending the text has no religious weight. It means describing that weight accurately. This is what the text says; this is how Jewish tradition reads it; this is how Christians read it; this is what scholars think; and here is my argument about the words.

Your classmates have read the same passages from different places. One may have heard Ruth chanted in Hebrew on Shavuot. Another may have heard Luke 15 preached. Another may have met the Bible for the first time this year. In Chicago, the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions put readers of many scriptures in one hall for the first time on that scale, and the city's neighborhoods still hold synagogues, churches, mosques and temples within blocks of each other. A classroom like yours is that hall in small. The rules you have practiced, attribute every belief, compare rather than judge, let disagreement stand, are what let it work.

For your reflection, write one page answering three questions. What did you learn to do this year that you could not do before: read in two translations, trace a word, tell a genre, cite a reader? Where did the course's neutrality feel hardest, and what did you do? And what will you carry out of the room: into an argument about a speech that quotes scripture, into a museum, into a conversation with someone whose tradition is not yours? The Bible will keep appearing in your life, in courts, songs, novels and elections. You now know how to read it, and how to hear how others read it.

words.d: describing a text and its readings accurately and fairly, without adopting or dismissing any of them
the Jewish festival of weeks, at which the book of Ruth is traditionally read
a gathering in Chicago in 1893 that brought representatives of many religions together on one platform
writing that looks back on what was learned, what was hard and what will be carried forward

look.title: The Hardest Moment
look.text: A student writes: 'When I argued that Isaiah 7:14 is about a child in Isaiah's own time, a classmate said I was denying that it is about Jesus. I was not sure how to answer without either backing down or telling him his church was wrong.'
look.prompt: Using the course's rules, write the answer the student could have given. What does it attribute, what does it compare, and what does it leave standing?

check.q: What does objectivity mean in this course?
choices: Pretending the Bible has no religious meaning
Treating the Bible as untrue
Describing the text and its readings accurately without adopting or dismissing any
Reading only the King James Version
check.why: Schempp permits objective study; the course defines it as accurate, attributed description of the text and its readers.

check.q: At which festival is Ruth traditionally read in synagogues?
choices: Shavuot
Passover
Yom Kippur
Hanukkah
check.why: Ruth is one of the five scrolls and is read on Shavuot, the harvest festival.

check.q: What happened in Chicago in 1893?
choices: The Supreme Court decided McCollum
The World's Parliament of Religions brought many traditions to one platform
The Moody Bible Institute printed the first Cherokee Bible
Handel's Messiah was first performed in America
check.why: The 1893 Parliament, held with the World's Columbian Exposition, gathered representatives of many religions; McCollum came from Champaign in 1948.

review.q: Which of these is the best size for a capstone passage?
choices: A single word
A whole book such as Romans
A self-contained unit such as a parable or a psalm
Two unrelated verses
review.why: A pericope, the unit the text marks off, is small enough to read closely and large enough to show how it works.

review.q: What kind of question does the capstone leave outside its scope?
choices: What a repeated word does
Whether the events happened or the text is the word of God
How two translations differ
How Rashi read a verse
review.why: Questions of historical fact and religious truth belong to history and faith; the capstone argues from the text.

review.q: Which translations may be quoted freely because they are in the public domain?
choices: NIV and NRSV
ESV and NJPS 1985
Any translation printed after 1990
KJV, ASV, WEB and JPS 1917
review.why: Those four are public domain; modern versions are copyrighted and should be paraphrased with a citation.

choices: A Hebrew word for loyal love or faithful kindness
A Greek word for word or reason
A festival at which Ruth is read
A pattern of mirrored lines
review.why: Hesed appears in Ruth 1:8, 2:20 and 3:10; logos is the Greek word, Shavuot the festival and chiasm the pattern.

review.q: How should a capstone present Rashi's reading of Ruth 1:16?
choices: As the correct meaning of the verse
As a mistaken medieval view
As a Jewish reading, attributed and stated in its own terms
As identical to the Christian reading
review.why: Every reading is attributed and described as its readers would recognize it; none is ranked above another.

review.q: Which sentence is a thesis about what a text does?
choices: Psalm 137 is upsetting
Psalm 137 proves God's justice
Psalm 137 was written in 586 BCE
Psalm 137 moves from memory to oath to curse, turning the pain of verse 1 outward
review.why: It names a feature of the text's shape and says what it accomplishes; the others are a reaction, a claim about God and an overconfident date.

review.q: What is the strongest kind of evidence in a close reading?
choices: The passage's own wording and structure
A commentator's opinion
A tradition's teaching
An archaeological date
review.why: The words and shape of the passage can be checked by any reader; the other kinds are weighed after it.

review.q: Why does the capstone rubric score fairness as heavily as evidence?
choices: Because evidence is hard to find
Because in a public school the course must describe every tradition accurately without adopting or dismissing it
Because teachers prefer polite essays
Because fairness replaces the need for a thesis
review.why: Objective study, as Schempp described it, depends on accurate attribution, so the rubric enforces it.
